question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?

sections.title: Conceptual Framework and Recent Interest
sections.text: The literature frames the integration of artificial intelligence into design processes as a shift toward treating intelligence as a fundamental resource for interaction designers [1]. This perspective has generated recent interest in utilizing AI, or more specifically Machine Learning (ML), as a design material for interaction, a trend highlighted by works from Dove et al. 2017, Hebron n.d., and Leahu 2016 [4]. By adopting this view, researchers aim to explore AI’s potential in improving interactions with apps and software systems [3]. To support this approach, advocates for 'design first' practices suggest a change in perspective, viewing the collection of AI algorithms as 'a toolbox of design materials' [2]. However, this valid and well-grounded view brings with it a need to better understand how intelligence functions as a design material [1].

question: How has the citation graph been used to improve neural language models for scientific papers?

sections.title: Challenges in Scientific Language Modeling
sections.text: Applying large language models to scientific domains remains difficult due to the unique characteristics of scientific language and knowledge [2]. Scientific texts are often dense with technical terminology, implicit assumptions, multimodal data representations, and tightly interlinked concepts that require deeper contextual comprehension [2]. To address these complexities, researchers have developed specialized evaluation frameworks and retrieval systems. For instance, SciCUEval was introduced as a comprehensive dataset for evaluating scientific context understanding in large language models [2]. Additionally, SciRAG was proposed as an adaptive, citation-aware, and outline-guided retrieval and synthesis framework for scientific literature [1]. This system specifically addresses whether papers use different formats of question-and-answer interactions with users to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to large language models [1].

sections.title: Leveraging Citation Graph Structure
sections.text: The citation graph provides unique structural information regarding document-level relatedness that can be utilized in tasks such as paper summarization, allowing models to explore beyond intra-document information [4]. In a citation graph, adjacent paper nodes share related scientific terms and topics, which serves as a basis for integrating external context [4]. This structural data is valuable because it highlights the importance of the citation graph in assisting the generation of high-quality summaries [3]. By incorporating this graph-based relatedness, models can better capture the interlinked nature of scientific concepts that standard text-only approaches might miss.

sections.title: Enhancing Information Extraction
sections.text: Citation graph information has been effectively integrated into neural scientific information extraction through models like CitationIE. This model can leverage either the structure of the citation graph or the content of citing and cited documents [5]. When this citation graph information is combined with document text, it leads to particularly strong improvements for salient entity classification and relation extraction [5]. Furthermore, this integration provides an increase in end-to-end information extraction system performance over strong baselines [5]. The ability to utilize both the structural connections and the textual content of related papers allows for more accurate identification of entities and relations within scientific documents.

question: How have open-source publishing platforms impacted the global distribution of academic publishing?

sections.title: Geographic Imbalance in Publishing
sections.text: The current academic publishing ecosystem is characterized by significant structural inequality. Most international journals with wide reach are located in Western countries, resulting in less distribution to the Global South and other regions [2]. This concentration means the broader ecosystem remains fairly unbalanced, with Western nations dominating the landscape of high-impact international journals [2]. Consequently, researchers in developing countries face barriers to visibility, although peer review boards have begun assisting in raising the quality of submissions from these regions to approach international standards [1].

sections.title: Open Source and Open Access Mechanisms
sections.text: The development of open-source software has fundamentally altered the infrastructure of academic publishing. The Open Source software movement enabled the creation of the OJS platform, which serves as a key tool for managing journals [1]. This technological shift, combined with the Open Access approach, provides an exemplar for moving academic publishing forward by opening up new routes to publication [1]. Furthermore, the CARPET platform addresses specific gaps by providing information on e-publishing technology and supporting the sustainability of existing e-publishing projects and their solutions [3]. These tools collectively lower the barriers to entry for new journals and support the operational continuity of established digital publishing initiatives.

sections.title: Disintermediation of Publisher Control
sections.text: The rise of open access, academic social networks, and piracy websites has eroded the total control publishers previously held over how academics access published content [4]. Open access publications can now proliferate across the web through the use of Creative Commons licenses, which allow for permission-free sharing of content without requiring mediation by publisher portals [4]. As a result, open access articles appear in a diverse range of locations, including faculty websites, institutional and subject repositories, and academic social networks, all of which legally circumvent traditional publisher portals [4]. This decentralization of distribution channels ensures that research is accessible through multiple independent avenues, reducing reliance on centralized commercial gatekeepers.

sections.title: Digital Transformation of Material Conditions
sections.text: The academic world is one arena in which digital publishing is having a particularly strong impact [5]. With the rise to prominence of digital publishing, the material conditions of book production, distribution, organization, and consumption are undergoing a rapid and potentially profound transformation [5]. This shift moves the industry away from physical constraints and toward a digital-first model, where the speed and reach of distribution are no longer limited by traditional logistical bottlenecks. The integration of open-source platforms and open access policies accelerates this transition, reshaping how knowledge is produced, shared, and consumed globally.

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations and Reorientation
sections.text: Distributed cognition (DC) has been proposed as a new foundation for human-computer interaction (HCI), offering a radical reorientation of how designers approach the field [6]. This theory is specifically tailored to understanding interactions among people and technologies, providing an effective theoretical foundation for understanding HCI and a fertile framework for designing and evaluating digital artifacts [5] [6]. At a very specific level, social constructivist theories of situated cognition and distributed cognition are fundamental to these concepts [4]. Theories from social psychology and cognitive science further provide diverse perspectives on group dynamics, adaptive behavior, and networks of social relationships [3]. A model visualizing different theoretical aspects of DC theory illustrates how cognitive-ingrained states propagate throughout a process, creating a cognitive feedback loop that leads to an architecture of cognition at the community level [3]. In this framework, one expects a system that can dynamically configure itself to bring subsystems into coordination to accomplish various functions [2]. Furthermore, DC is compatible with different users encountering different features of the same experience [1].

question: How is artificial intelligence being utilized to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of sleep apnea?

sections.title: Clinical Context and Diagnostic Challenges
sections.text: Sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (SAHS) is a chronic and highly prevalent disease considered a major health problem in industrialized countries [2]. Despite advocacy in the last decade for the development and adoption of new diagnostic methods, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains underdiagnosed and untreated in a significant number of adult patients [3]. The current gold standard for diagnosis is in-laboratory nocturnal polysomnography (PSG) [2]. This diagnostic process involves identifying sleep stages in an overnight polysomnogram (PSG) which utilizes EEG modality to detect issues such as problems with initiating sleep, insomnia, and sleep apnea syndrome (SAS) [1]. However, the traditional visual scoring of these stages suffers from inherent subjectivity and inter-rater variability [1].

sections.title: Cardiac Screening and AI-Driven Treatment
sections.text: Beyond standard polysomnography, artificial intelligence is being applied to cardiac data for screening.
